dx: Lateral epicondylitis (tendinopathy of the extensor carpi radialis brevis origin)
case: A 46-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 4-month history of pain over the outer aspect of his right elbow. He installs drywall and uses a power screwdriver for most of the workday. The pain is worse when he grips tools or lifts a cup with the palm facing down. He recalls no injury. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows tenderness 1 cm distal to the right lateral epicondyle. Resisted extension of the wrist with the elbow extended reproduces the pain. Elbow range of motion is full, and there is no swelling or warmth. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate is 8 mm/h (normal 0 to 15). Ultrasonography shows a thickened, hypoechoic common extensor tendon origin. Diagnosis: lateral epicondylitis.

questions.stem: Eight months later, his symptoms persist despite rest and physical therapy, and the diseased tendon origin is surgically debrided. Which of the following findings is most likely on microscopic examination of the excised tissue?
options: Sheets of neutrophils with liquefactive necrosis of the tendon
Disorganized collagen, new vessels, and scant inflammation
Urate crystal deposits rimmed by foreign body giant cells
Noncaseating granulomas with multinucleated giant cells
approach: Note the clues: months of overuse pain, no warmth or swelling, and a normal sedimentation rate.
Recognize chronic tendinopathy as a degenerative process (tendinosis) more than an inflammatory one.
Pick the histology of failed repair: disorganized collagen, fibroblasts, and small vessels with few inflammatory cells.
questions.why: Lateral epicondylitis is overuse tendinopathy at the origin of the extensor carpi radialis brevis. Repeated small tears outpace repair, so the tendon shows tendinosis: collagen fibers that are thin, loosely packed, and out of line, more ground substance, many fibroblasts, and ingrowth of small vessels. Inflammatory cells are scarce, which is why the term epicondylitis is a misnomer and why his sedimentation rate is normal.
whyNot: Neutrophils with liquefactive necrosis describe an abscess, as in septic bursitis or a tendon sheath infection. He has no warmth, swelling, or systemic signs.
Correct.
Urate crystals with giant cells form a tophus in chronic gout. Gout causes episodic, warm, inflamed joints, which he does not have.
Noncaseating granulomas suggest sarcoidosis or a foreign body reaction. Overuse tendinopathy does not form granulomas.

questions.stem: Analysis of the debrided tendon shows that much of its normal collagen has been replaced by thinner fibrils of the collagen type that predominates in early granulation tissue. This collagen type is also the main component of which of the following?
options: Lamina densa of epithelial basement membranes
Lamellar bone of the lateral epicondyle
Hyaline cartilage of the articular surface
Reticular fiber network of lymph nodes
approach: Identify the collagen of early granulation tissue as type III.
Recall where type III collagen is normally found: reticular fibers, blood vessel walls, and early scar.
Match type III collagen to the reticular framework of lymphoid organs.
questions.why: Healthy tendon is built mostly of thick, parallel type I collagen fibrils, which give it high tensile strength. Repair tissue in tendinopathy contains more type III collagen, which forms thinner, weaker fibrils, the same collagen laid down first in granulation tissue. Type III collagen also forms reticular fibers, the fine supporting mesh of lymph nodes, spleen, bone marrow, and liver, and it is abundant in blood vessel walls.
whyNot: The lamina densa of basement membranes is made of type IV collagen, which forms a sheet-like network. Defects in type IV collagen cause Alport syndrome.
Bone matrix is mainly type I collagen, the same collagen that normally makes up healthy tendon.
Hyaline cartilage contains mainly type II collagen, which is also found in the nucleus pulposus and vitreous humor.
Correct.

questions.stem: He asks why the tendon is still painful even though he took 6 weeks off work. Which of the following features of the tendon best explains its slow healing?
options: Sparse blood supply and low cell density
Absence of resident collagen-producing cells
Continuous bathing of the tendon in synovial fluid
A matrix built mainly of type II collagen
approach: Recall that repair needs cells to make new matrix and blood to deliver nutrients and more cells.
Tendons have few cells (tenocytes) and a poor blood supply, especially near the bony origin.
Choose the option that combines low vascularity with low cellularity.
questions.why: Tendon is dense regular connective tissue with relatively few tenocytes (specialized fibroblasts) spread between thick collagen bundles. Its blood supply enters mainly at the muscle junction, the bone attachment, and the surrounding paratenon, and the region near the bony origin is poorly vascular. With few cells to make new matrix and little blood to bring nutrients and repair cells, tendon heals over months. Articular cartilage has no blood vessels at all and heals even more poorly.
whyNot: Correct.
Tendons do contain collagen-producing cells, the tenocytes. They are few in number, so repair is slow, but they are present.
Bathing in synovial fluid hampers healing of intra-articular structures such as the anterior cruciate ligament. The common extensor origin lies outside the elbow joint.
Type II collagen is the main collagen of hyaline cartilage. Tendon matrix is mainly type I collagen.

questions.stem: To measure grip strength, the physician asks him to squeeze a dynamometer with the wrist held first in slight extension and then in full flexion. Grip force is much lower with the wrist fully flexed, on both the affected and the unaffected side. Which of the following best explains the lower force with the wrist flexed?
options: Fewer finger flexor motor units can be recruited in this position
Finger flexor sarcomeres are stretched beyond optimal filament overlap
Finger flexor sarcomeres are too short for optimal filament overlap
Finger flexors contract at a higher velocity, which lowers force
approach: The long finger flexors cross the front of the wrist, so wrist flexion shortens them.
Apply the length-tension relationship: force is greatest at a sarcomere length with optimal actin and myosin overlap.
At very short lengths, thin filaments overlap each other and thick filaments press on the Z discs, so fewer cross-bridges form.
questions.why: The flexor digitorum superficialis and profundus pass in front of the wrist. Flexing the wrist shortens them before the grip starts, so their sarcomeres work below optimal length, where thin filaments overlap and fewer cross-bridges can form. This is called active insufficiency. During a normal grip, the wrist extensors, including the extensor carpi radialis brevis, hold the wrist slightly extended to keep the finger flexors near optimal length, which is why gripping loads his painful tendon.
whyNot: Motor unit recruitment depends on the drive from the motor neuron pool and does not fall because of wrist position. The loss of force appears on the healthy side too.
Overstretching reduces overlap between thick and thin filaments and lowers force, but wrist flexion shortens the finger flexors. Wrist extension combined with finger extension would stretch them.
Correct.
Velocity lowers force only when a muscle is shortening. A dynamometer grip is nearly isometric, so velocity is close to zero in both wrist positions.

dx: Autosomal recessive osteopetrosis from carbonic anhydrase II deficiency
case: An 18-month-old boy is brought to the physician because of a fracture of the right femur after he fell from a sitting position. He has had poor weight gain since infancy. His parents are first cousins. His length and weight are below the 3rd percentile. Laboratory studies show a serum sodium concentration of 138 mEq/L (normal 135 to 145), chloride 114 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106), and bicarbonate 14 mEq/L (normal 22 to 28), with a urine pH of 6.8. Radiographs show diffusely increased bone density and a bone-within-bone appearance of the vertebrae. CT of the head shows calcifications in the basal ganglia. Diagnosis: autosomal recessive osteopetrosis caused by carbonic anhydrase II deficiency.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the increased bone density in this patient?
options: Excess calcitonin secretion suppresses osteoclast activity
Osteoblasts lay down excess osteoid that mineralizes too rapidly
Osteoclast precursors cannot form because RANKL is absent
Osteoclasts cannot acidify the space beneath the ruffled border
approach: Recall the reaction carbonic anhydrase II catalyzes: carbon dioxide and water to carbonic acid, a source of hydrogen ions.
Osteoclasts pump these hydrogen ions into the resorption pit to dissolve hydroxyapatite.
Without the enzyme, bone is not resorbed and accumulates, even though osteoclasts are present.
questions.why: Osteoclasts dissolve bone mineral by secreting acid into the sealed space under the ruffled border (Howship lacuna). Carbonic anhydrase II in the osteoclast makes the hydrogen ions that the vacuolar proton pump moves into this space. Without it, mineral is not dissolved, old bone and calcified cartilage are not removed, and the skeleton becomes dense but brittle. The same enzyme is needed in the renal tubules, which explains his normal anion gap metabolic acidosis with an inappropriately alkaline urine.
whyNot: Calcitonin has only a minor role in human bone, and calcitonin excess, as in medullary thyroid carcinoma, does not cause osteopetrosis.
Osteopetrosis is a disease of too little resorption. Osteoblast bone formation is not the primary problem.
RANKL deficiency is a real but rare cause of osteopetrosis in which osteoclasts are nearly absent. It does not cause renal tubular acidosis, which points to carbonic anhydrase II deficiency here.
Correct.

questions.stem: At the age of 3 years, he has trouble finding toys across a room. His pupils react sluggishly to light, and funduscopic examination shows pale optic discs. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his visual loss?
options: Compression of the optic nerves in narrowed bony canals
Calcification of the occipital cortex causing cortical blindness
Autoimmune demyelination of the optic nerves
Retinal ganglion cell loss from chronic metabolic acidosis
approach: Pale optic discs and a sluggish pupillary light reflex localize the problem to the optic nerves.
In osteopetrosis, unresorbed bone narrows the skull foramina and canals.
Link narrowing of the optic canals to compression and atrophy of the optic nerves.
questions.why: Bone that cannot be remodeled keeps thickening, so the canals and foramina of the skull base become narrow. Nerves passing through them are compressed, causing optic atrophy and vision loss, hearing loss, and facial nerve palsy. Encroachment of bone on the marrow space can also cause anemia or pancytopenia with extramedullary hematopoiesis and hepatosplenomegaly. These complications are most frequent and most severe in the infantile autosomal recessive forms.
whyNot: Correct.
Cortical blindness spares the pupillary light reflex and leaves the optic discs normal, because the lesion lies behind the lateral geniculate body.
Optic neuritis from demyelination usually affects older children and adults and is often painful. It is unrelated to osteopetrosis.
Metabolic acidosis from renal tubular acidosis affects growth and bone, but it does not destroy retinal ganglion cells.

questions.stem: A bone biopsy shows many large multinucleated cells lying in shallow pits on the bone surface. These cells arise from which of the following?
options: Mesenchymal stromal cells of the bone marrow
Osteocytes released from their lacunae
Monocyte and macrophage precursors
Chondrocytes of the growth plate
approach: Identify the cells: large, multinucleated, and sitting in pits on the bone surface. These are osteoclasts.
Recall that osteoclasts form by fusion of hematopoietic precursors.
Separate this lineage from the mesenchymal lineage that gives osteoblasts and osteocytes.
questions.why: Osteoclasts form when monocyte and macrophage precursors fuse under the influence of M-CSF and RANKL, which osteoblasts and stromal cells supply. The mature cell is multinucleated, seals onto bone, and resorbs it with acid and cathepsin K in a Howship lacuna. In carbonic anhydrase II deficiency the osteoclasts are present but cannot make enough acid. Because osteoclasts come from blood-forming stem cells, hematopoietic stem cell transplantation can correct some severe infantile forms of osteopetrosis.
whyNot: Mesenchymal stromal cells give rise to osteoblasts, chondrocytes, and fat cells. Osteoblasts are mononuclear and secrete type I collagen and alkaline phosphatase.
Osteocytes are osteoblasts trapped in mineralized matrix. They are small, single-nucleus cells that sense mechanical load and secrete FGF23.
Correct.
Growth plate chondrocytes build the cartilage model for long bone growth. They do not resorb bone.

questions.stem: At the age of 2 years, he develops diffuse muscle weakness during an episode of gastroenteritis with diarrhea. Deep tendon reflexes are decreased. Serum potassium concentration is 2.4 mEq/L (normal 3.5 to 5.0). Which of the following best explains his weakness?
options: Sustained depolarization inactivates muscle sodium channels
Muscle cells are hyperpolarized farther from threshold
Nerve sodium channels open with less depolarization
Less acetylcholine is released at each motor end plate
approach: Identify the cause of the low potassium: urinary potassium loss from his renal tubular acidosis, made worse by diarrhea.
Apply the Nernst equation: lower extracellular potassium makes the resting membrane potential more negative.
A more negative resting potential sits farther from threshold, so muscle fibers are harder to fire and he is weak.
questions.why: The resting membrane potential of nerve and muscle depends mostly on the potassium gradient across the membrane. When extracellular potassium falls, the gradient grows and the resting potential becomes more negative (hyperpolarized), so a larger stimulus is needed to reach threshold. Muscle fibers fire less easily, which causes weakness and low reflexes. Renal tubular acidosis from carbonic anhydrase II deficiency wastes potassium in the urine, and diarrhea adds more loss. High potassium also causes weakness, but by a different route: sustained depolarization keeps sodium channels inactivated.
whyNot: Sustained depolarization with sodium channel inactivation is how hyperkalemia causes weakness. His potassium is low.
Correct.
A lower threshold for sodium channel opening is the effect of hypocalcemia, which causes tetany and spasms instead of weakness.
Reduced acetylcholine release causes weakness in Lambert-Eaton syndrome and hypermagnesemia. Low potassium acts on the muscle membrane itself.

case: A 17-year-old boy comes to the physician for a preparticipation sports examination before joining his high school basketball team. His father died suddenly at the age of 36 years. He is 198 cm (6 ft 6 in) tall, and his arm span is 208 cm. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows long, thin fingers, pectus excavatum, a high-arched palate, and mild thoracic scoliosis. A midsystolic click is heard at the apex. Slit-lamp examination shows upward and outward displacement of both lenses. Echocardiography shows a dilated aortic root and mitral valve prolapse. Diagnosis: Marfan syndrome.

questions.stem: Genetic testing shows a heterozygous missense mutation in FBN1. Which of the following mechanisms contributes most to the progressive dilation of his aortic root?
options: Excess TGF-beta activity from defective microfibrils
Defective triple helix formation in type I collagen
Reduced lysyl oxidase cross-linking from copper deficiency
Haploinsufficiency of elastin from a 7q11.23 deletion
approach: FBN1 encodes fibrillin-1, the main protein of extracellular microfibrils.
Microfibrils normally bind latent TGF-beta and keep it inactive.
Defective microfibrils release too much active TGF-beta, which weakens the aortic media.
questions.why: Marfan syndrome is autosomal dominant, caused by mutations in FBN1 on chromosome 15. Fibrillin-1 microfibrils are the scaffold for elastic fibers and also hold latent TGF-beta in the matrix. When fibrillin-1 is abnormal, TGF-beta is activated in excess, which promotes matrix breakdown and loss of smooth muscle in the aortic media (cystic medial degeneration). The aortic root dilates, and the risk of aortic dissection rises. Excess TGF-beta activity also contributes to the skeletal overgrowth.
whyNot: Correct.
Defective type I collagen triple helices cause osteogenesis imperfecta, with fractures and blue sclerae.
Lysyl oxidase needs copper, and its failure in Menkes disease weakens collagen and elastin. Copper metabolism is normal in Marfan syndrome.
Deletion at 7q11.23 that includes the elastin gene causes Williams syndrome, which narrows the aorta above the valve (supravalvular aortic stenosis).

questions.stem: Homocystinuria can produce a similar tall, thin body habitus. Which of the following findings would most strongly favor homocystinuria in a tall patient with long fingers?
options: Prolapse of the mitral valve with a midsystolic apical click
Arm span exceeding height with long, slender fingers and toes
Downward lens displacement and a prior venous thrombosis
Pectus excavatum with a high-arched palate and scoliosis
approach: List what both disorders share: tall stature, long limbs and digits, and chest deformity.
Find the features that separate them: lens direction, thrombosis, and intellectual disability.
Pick the combination that only homocystinuria explains.
questions.why: Both disorders cause a marfanoid habitus and lens dislocation. In Marfan syndrome the lens usually moves up and out, and the main threats are aortic root dilation, aortic dissection, and mitral valve prolapse. In homocystinuria, most often from cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency, the lens usually moves down and in, and high homocysteine damages endothelium, causing arterial and venous thrombosis. Intellectual disability is also common in homocystinuria and is not a feature of Marfan syndrome.
whyNot: Mitral valve prolapse is a typical cardiovascular finding in Marfan syndrome. It points away from homocystinuria.
Long limbs and digits are part of the marfanoid habitus seen in both disorders, so they do not separate them.
Correct.
Pectus deformity, a high-arched palate, and scoliosis occur in both disorders as part of the skeletal overgrowth.

questions.stem: The same gene defect affects the yellow ligaments that connect the laminae of adjacent vertebrae and recoil as the spine straightens after flexion. Which of the following best describes the normal fibers responsible for this recoil?
options: Type I collagen fibrils cross-linked by lysyl oxidase
Elastin cores built on fibrillin microfibrils
Type II collagen fibrils embedded in aggrecan
Type III collagen fibers forming a reticular mesh
approach: Identify the yellow ligaments as the ligamenta flava, which are rich in elastic fibers.
Recall how an elastic fiber is built: an amorphous elastin core around a sheath of microfibrils.
Link the microfibril protein to the FBN1 defect.
questions.why: The ligamenta flava are yellow because they are rich in elastic fibers, which let them stretch during flexion and recoil during extension. An elastic fiber forms when tropoelastin is laid down on a scaffold of fibrillin-1 microfibrils and then cross-linked into an elastin core. Fibrillin microfibrils also bind latent TGF-beta and hold it inactive in the matrix. Elastic fibers are also prominent in the aortic media and the suspensory ligaments of the lens, which explains the aortic and lens findings in Marfan syndrome.
whyNot: Type I collagen fibrils give tensile strength to tendon, ligament, and bone, but collagen does not stretch and recoil the way elastic fibers do.
Correct.
Type II collagen with aggrecan forms hyaline cartilage, which resists compression.
Type III collagen forms reticular fibers in lymphoid organs and vessel walls. They support cells but do not provide elastic recoil.

questions.stem: When he folds his thumb across his palm and closes his fingers over it, the tip of the thumb extends well beyond the ulnar border of the hand. Movement at the first carpometacarpal joint contributes to this sign. Which of the following best describes this joint?
options: Plane joint between the capitate and first metacarpal
Condyloid joint between the scaphoid and first metacarpal
Hinge joint between the trapezoid and first metacarpal
Saddle joint between the trapezium and first metacarpal
approach: Identify the bones of the first carpometacarpal joint: the trapezium and the base of the first metacarpal.
Recall that both surfaces are concave in one direction and convex in the other.
Classify this as a saddle joint, which allows flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, and opposition.
questions.why: The first carpometacarpal joint lies between the trapezium and the base of the first metacarpal. Each surface is shaped like a saddle, so the joint moves in two planes and adds some rotation, which allows opposition of the thumb. In Marfan syndrome, long digits and joint laxity let the thumb tip pass beyond the ulnar border of the closed hand, the thumb sign. Other synovial joint types include the pivot (atlantoaxial), hinge (interphalangeal), condyloid (radiocarpal), ball and socket (shoulder), and plane (intercarpal).
whyNot: The capitate articulates with the third metacarpal. Plane joints, such as the intercarpal joints, allow only gliding.
The scaphoid does not articulate with the first metacarpal. Condyloid joints, such as the radiocarpal and metacarpophalangeal joints, have an oval head in an oval socket.
The trapezoid articulates with the second metacarpal. Hinge joints, such as the elbow and interphalangeal joints, move in one plane.
Correct.

case: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of frequent falls and difficulty climbing stairs over the past year. He walked at 18 months of age. His mother's brother used a wheelchair from the age of 11 years and died of respiratory failure at 20 years. Physical examination shows a waddling gait, firm, enlarged calves, and weakness of the hip and shoulder girdle muscles. To rise from the floor, he pushes on his knees and thighs with his hands. Serum creatine kinase activity is 16,800 U/L (normal 40 to 200). Diagnosis: Duchenne muscular dystrophy.

questions.stem: Which of the following findings is most likely on biopsy of his enlarged calf muscle?
options: Perifascicular atrophy with perivascular inflammation
Uniformly enlarged fibers with normal architecture
Necrotic fibers replaced by fat and fibrous tissue
Endomysial CD8 T cells invading nonnecrotic fibers
approach: Notice that the calves are large while he is weak.
Recall that absent dystrophin makes the sarcolemma tear with contraction, so fibers die repeatedly.
Dead fibers are replaced by fat and connective tissue, which enlarges the calf without adding strength (pseudohypertrophy).
questions.why: Dystrophin links the actin cytoskeleton through the dystroglycan complex to the extracellular matrix. Without it, the sarcolemma tears during contraction, calcium floods in, and fibers undergo necrosis. Regeneration cannot keep up, so the biopsy shows fibers of varied size, necrotic and regenerating fibers, and progressive replacement by fat and fibrous tissue. The calves enlarge from this fibrofatty tissue, which is pseudohypertrophy. Creatine kinase leaking from damaged fibers explains the very high serum level.
whyNot: Perifascicular atrophy with perivascular inflammation is typical of dermatomyositis, an inflammatory myopathy with a heliotrope rash and Gottron papules.
Uniformly large, normal fibers describe true hypertrophy, as after resistance training. His large calves are weak, which points to pseudohypertrophy.
Correct.
CD8 T cells invading fibers are typical of polymyositis, which presents in adults. A family history in a maternal uncle points to an X-linked dystrophy.

questions.stem: Genetic testing shows a deletion of several exons of the DMD gene whose combined length is not a multiple of three nucleotides. Which of the following best explains why this deletion causes his severe phenotype?
options: It shifts the reading frame, creating an early stop codon
It removes the promoter so that no mRNA is transcribed
It yields a shortened protein that keeps both binding ends
It produces a protein that blocks the normal allele's product
approach: Codons are read three nucleotides at a time.
Deleting a number of nucleotides that is not divisible by three shifts the reading frame downstream.
A frameshift soon creates a stop codon, so no functional dystrophin is made, which gives Duchenne dystrophy.
questions.why: The reading frame rule explains most of the difference between Duchenne and Becker dystrophy. A frameshift deletion scrambles every codon after the break and soon reaches a premature stop codon, so the mRNA is degraded and no functional dystrophin is made. An in-frame deletion removes some codons but keeps the rest of the message in register, so a shorter, partly working dystrophin is made, which gives the milder Becker form. The DMD gene is one of the largest human genes, which is why new mutations are common.
whyNot: Correct.
The deletion described lies within the coding exons. Promoter deletions are uncommon, and the key here is that the deleted length is not divisible by three.
A shortened protein that keeps the actin-binding and dystroglycan-binding ends results from an in-frame deletion and causes Becker dystrophy.
A boy has only one X chromosome and therefore one DMD allele. Dominant-negative effects require a normal allele whose product can be disrupted.

questions.stem: At the age of 17 years, he has morning headaches and daytime sleepiness. When he lies supine, his abdomen moves inward as he inhales. Weakness of which of the following muscles, with its nerve supply, best explains this finding?
options: Sternocleidomastoid, spinal accessory nerve (CN XI)
External intercostals, intercostal nerves from T1 to T11
Rectus abdominis, thoracoabdominal nerves from T7 to T11
Diaphragm, phrenic nerves from C3 to C5
approach: Normally the diaphragm descends during inspiration and pushes the abdominal wall outward.
Inward movement of the abdomen during inspiration (paradoxical breathing) means the diaphragm is weak and is being pulled up by negative chest pressure.
Name the diaphragm's nerve supply: the phrenic nerves from C3 to C5.
questions.why: The diaphragm is the main muscle of inspiration. When it contracts, it descends and pushes the abdominal contents down and the abdominal wall out. When it is weak, the accessory muscles expand the chest, the negative pressure pulls the diaphragm upward, and the abdomen moves in, especially when lying supine. Diaphragm weakness causes hypoventilation during sleep, with morning headaches from carbon dioxide retention and daytime sleepiness. Respiratory failure and dilated cardiomyopathy are the main causes of death in Duchenne dystrophy.
whyNot: The sternocleidomastoid is an accessory muscle that raises the sternum in forced inspiration. Paradoxical abdominal motion points to the diaphragm.
The external intercostals help raise the ribs in inspiration, but their weakness does not make the abdomen move inward when he lies supine.
The rectus abdominis flexes the trunk and helps forced expiration. Its weakness does not cause inward abdominal motion during inspiration.
Correct.

questions.stem: His findings are compared with those of an unrelated 16-year-old boy who first had exercise-induced calf cramps at the age of 11 years, still walks independently, and has a serum creatine kinase activity of 4,200 U/L. Which of the following results of dystrophin immunostaining is most likely in the older boy's muscle?
options: No staining at the sarcolemma of nearly all fibers
Faint, patchy staining at the sarcolemma of most fibers
Normal, continuous staining at the sarcolemma of all fibers
Strong staining confined to the myofiber nuclei
approach: Later onset, slower course, and walking in the teens point to Becker dystrophy.
Becker dystrophy makes a reduced amount of a shortened dystrophin.
Immunostaining therefore shows reduced, uneven staining along the fiber membrane, instead of the absent staining of Duchenne.
questions.why: Becker muscular dystrophy is the milder form of the same X-linked disease. Symptoms start later, often in late childhood or adolescence, many patients walk into adulthood, and creatine kinase is high but usually lower than in Duchenne. Because some shortened dystrophin is made, immunostaining of the sarcolemma is faint and patchy, and Western blot shows protein of reduced size or amount. In Duchenne dystrophy, staining is absent from nearly all fibers. Genetic testing then shows whether the deletion keeps or shifts the reading frame.
whyNot: Absent staining in nearly all fibers is the Duchenne pattern, as in the younger boy. The older boy's later onset and preserved walking point to Becker dystrophy.
Correct.
Normal dystrophin staining would point to another myopathy, such as a limb-girdle dystrophy, which can look similar clinically.
Dystrophin is a cytoskeletal protein that sits under the sarcolemma. It is not a nuclear protein.

case: A 31-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 3-year history of difficulty releasing her grip on door handles and tools and frequent tripping. She had cataract surgery in both eyes at the age of 29 years. Her mother developed cataracts in her 50s and has no weakness. Physical examination shows bilateral ptosis, a long, thin face with wasting of the temporal muscles, weakness of neck flexion, and bilateral foot drop. After a firm handshake, she opens her hand slowly. Percussion of the thenar eminence causes a sustained contraction. An ECG shows a PR interval of 240 msec (normal 120 to 200). Diagnosis: myotonic dystrophy type 1.

questions.stem: Two years later, she gives birth to a boy after a pregnancy complicated by polyhydramnios. At birth he is severely hypotonic, has facial weakness, and needs ventilatory support. Which of the following best explains why his disease is more severe than his mother's?
options: Inheritance of a second mutant DMPK allele from the father
High mutant mitochondrial DNA load inherited from the oocyte
Imprinting that silences the normal paternal DMPK allele
Further expansion of the CTG repeat during transmission
approach: Notice the pattern across three generations: cataracts only in the grandmother, adult disease in the mother, and severe newborn disease in the son.
Earlier onset and greater severity in each generation is anticipation.
Anticipation in myotonic dystrophy comes from an unstable CTG repeat that grows when passed on, most dramatically through the mother.
questions.why: Myotonic dystrophy type 1 is autosomal dominant and caused by an expanded CTG repeat in the untranslated end of the DMPK gene on chromosome 19. The repeat is unstable and tends to grow in each generation, so onset is earlier and disease is more severe (anticipation). The largest expansions, which cause congenital myotonic dystrophy with hypotonia and breathing failure, are passed on almost always by an affected mother. The expanded RNA traps splicing regulators, causing missplicing of the muscle chloride channel and other proteins, which explains myotonia, weakness, cataracts, and conduction block.
whyNot: Nothing suggests the father is affected, and one expanded allele is enough to cause disease. A second mutant allele is not needed to explain the severity.
Mitochondrial disorders are passed through the mother and vary with mutant load, but myotonic dystrophy is a nuclear gene disorder with autosomal dominant inheritance.
Imprinting explains disorders such as Prader-Willi and Angelman syndromes. One expanded DMPK allele is enough to cause disease, whatever the parent of origin.
Correct.

questions.stem: Wasting of her temporal and masseter muscles gives her face a narrow, hollow appearance. From which pharyngeal arch do these muscles develop, and which nerve supplies them?
options: Second arch, facial nerve (CN VII)
First arch, mandibular nerve (CN V3)
Third arch, glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX)
Fourth arch, superior laryngeal nerve (CN X)
approach: Identify the temporalis and masseter as muscles of mastication.
Recall that the muscles of mastication come from the first pharyngeal arch.
Each arch keeps its own cranial nerve, and the first arch nerve is the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve.
questions.why: Each pharyngeal arch forms muscles that keep the nerve of that arch. The first arch forms the muscles of mastication (temporalis, masseter, medial and lateral pterygoids), plus the mylohyoid, anterior belly of the digastric, tensor tympani, and tensor veli palatini, all supplied by the mandibular nerve (CN V3). Wasting of the temporalis and masseter is typical of myotonic dystrophy and produces the long, narrow face. Her ptosis comes from weakness of the levator palpebrae superioris, which is supplied by the oculomotor nerve.
whyNot: The second arch forms the muscles of facial expression, the stapedius, the stylohyoid, and the posterior belly of the digastric, supplied by the facial nerve.
Correct.
The third arch forms only the stylopharyngeus, supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve.
The fourth arch forms the cricothyroid and most pharyngeal constrictors, supplied by branches of the vagus nerve.

questions.stem: Her weakness of neck flexion is accompanied by thin sternocleidomastoid muscles. Which of the following correctly describes the nerve supply and an action of one of these muscles?
options: Accessory nerve; turns the face toward the opposite side
Accessory nerve; turns the face toward the same side as the muscle
Ansa cervicalis; depresses the hyoid bone during swallowing
Facial nerve; tenses the skin of the anterior neck
approach: Recall the sternocleidomastoid's attachments: mastoid process above, sternum and clavicle below.
Contracting one side pulls the mastoid toward the same-side clavicle, which tilts the head toward that side and turns the face to the other side.
Name its motor nerve: the spinal accessory nerve (CN XI).
questions.why: The sternocleidomastoid runs from the mastoid process to the manubrium and the medial clavicle. One muscle acting alone tilts the head toward its own side and rotates the face toward the opposite side. Both muscles together flex the neck. Motor supply is the spinal accessory nerve (CN XI), which also supplies the trapezius. Weakness and wasting of the sternocleidomastoid with neck flexion weakness is a typical early finding in myotonic dystrophy type 1.
whyNot: Correct.
This reverses the rotation. Because the muscle pulls the mastoid process down and forward, the face turns away from the contracting side.
The ansa cervicalis supplies the infrahyoid muscles, such as the sternohyoid and omohyoid, which depress the hyoid.
The facial nerve supplies the platysma, which tenses the skin of the neck. The platysma is a muscle of facial expression.

questions.stem: Her skeletal muscles stay contracted after a voluntary grip, yet her ventricles relax fully between beats even during the tachycardia of exercise. Which of the following properties of cardiac muscle prevents its contractions from summating into tetany?
options: Absence of ryanodine receptors on the sarcoplasmic reticulum
Gap junctions that make the myocardium contract as a syncytium
A refractory period that lasts almost as long as contraction
Contraction triggered only by calcium entering from outside the cell
approach: Tetany needs a new action potential to arrive before the muscle relaxes.
The cardiac action potential has a long plateau from calcium entry through L-type channels.
Its refractory period lasts through most of the contraction, so a second contraction cannot be added on top of the first.
questions.why: In skeletal muscle the action potential lasts a few milliseconds, much shorter than the twitch, so repeated stimuli can summate into tetanus. In ventricular muscle the plateau of the action potential keeps sodium channels inactivated for most of systole, so the absolute refractory period lasts nearly as long as the contraction itself. A new beat cannot start until the muscle is relaxing, which protects filling. Her myotonia is different: missplicing of the skeletal muscle chloride channel leaves the membrane prone to repetitive firing, so the muscle keeps contracting after the voluntary effort ends.
whyNot: Cardiac muscle has ryanodine receptors (RyR2). Calcium entering through L-type channels opens them, releasing calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum (calcium-induced calcium release).
Gap junctions do spread excitation so the ventricles contract as a unit, but they do not stop one contraction from summating with the next.
Correct.
Most of the calcium for cardiac contraction comes from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Calcium entering from outside mainly acts as a trigger for that release.

dx: Type I osteogenesis imperfecta in a toddler evaluated for abuse
case: A 20-month-old girl is brought to the emergency department because she would not use her right arm after a fall from a low couch. Her father had several fractures in childhood and began to lose his hearing in his 30s. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows blue-gray sclerae, a swollen, tender right upper arm, and mildly lax joints. Radiographs show a transverse fracture of the middle third of the right humeral shaft. A skeletal survey shows generalized osteopenia, a healed fracture of the left tibia, and many small extra bones within the lambdoid suture. A child protection evaluation is started. Diagnosis: osteogenesis imperfecta type I.

questions.stem: Which of the following additional findings on the skeletal survey would most strongly suggest nonaccidental trauma instead of her bone disease?
options: Anterior bowing of both femurs and both tibias
Corner fractures of the distal femoral metaphyses
Thin cortices and slender shafts of the long bones
Compression and wedging of several vertebral bodies
approach: List the features already pointing to osteogenesis imperfecta: blue sclerae, wormian bones, osteopenia, and an affected father.
Recall the fracture patterns that are highly specific for abuse: classic metaphyseal lesions and posterior rib fractures.
Pick the finding produced by shaking or twisting forces that bone fragility alone rarely explains.
questions.why: Osteogenesis imperfecta and child abuse both cause multiple fractures, and the two must be told apart carefully. Clues for osteogenesis imperfecta include blue or gray sclerae, dentinogenesis imperfecta, wormian bones, osteopenia, bowing, and a family history of fractures or early hearing loss. Clues for abuse include classic metaphyseal lesions (corner or bucket-handle fractures), posterior rib fractures, fractures of different ages without a fitting history, and bruising in protected areas, usually in bone of normal density. Both can occur together, so the evaluation continues even when osteogenesis imperfecta is confirmed.
whyNot: Long bone bowing results from repeated microfractures in weak bone and is typical of osteogenesis imperfecta.
Correct.
Thin cortices and slender shafts reflect too little type I collagen matrix. They support osteogenesis imperfecta.
Vertebral compression fractures are common in osteogenesis imperfecta because of low bone mass.

questions.stem: Her primary teeth are gray-brown and translucent and wear down quickly. Which of the following best explains these dental findings?
options: Tetracycline bound to developing tooth mineral
Defective amelogenin in the developing enamel
Abnormal type I collagen in the dentin matrix
Excess fluoride built into enamel crystals
approach: Recall that the organic matrix of dentin, like bone, is mainly type I collagen.
Osteogenesis imperfecta is a type I collagen disorder, so dentin is abnormal (dentinogenesis imperfecta).
Weak dentin looks translucent and gray-brown, and the enamel on top chips off, so teeth wear quickly.
questions.why: Osteogenesis imperfecta is caused by mutations in COL1A1 or COL1A2, the genes for type I collagen. Every tissue rich in type I collagen is affected: bone (fractures with little trauma), sclera (thin, so the dark choroid shows through as blue), dentin (dentinogenesis imperfecta), ligaments (joint laxity), and the middle ear ossicles (conductive hearing loss, often starting in early adulthood, as in her father). Enamel contains no collagen, though it chips away from the weak dentin beneath it.
whyNot: Tetracycline taken while teeth are forming stains them yellow to brown in bands. It does not cause fractures or blue sclerae.
Amelogenin defects cause amelogenesis imperfecta, a disorder of enamel with normal dentin and normal bones.
Correct.
Excess fluoride causes dental fluorosis, with white or brown mottling of enamel. It does not weaken bone in childhood.

questions.stem: Genetic testing shows a heterozygous COL1A1 mutation that creates a premature stop codon, and the mutant mRNA is destroyed by nonsense-mediated decay. Which of the following best explains why her disease is milder than osteogenesis imperfecta caused by a glycine substitution in the triple helix?
options: Mutant chains enter triple helices and disrupt most of them
The normal allele doubles its output and fully compensates
The mutation affects only collagen made by osteoblasts
Collagen is made in half the usual amount but is normal
approach: Note that her mutant mRNA is destroyed, so no mutant chains are made.
Only the normal allele produces chains, so collagen is reduced in amount but normal in structure (haploinsufficiency).
Compare glycine substitutions, where abnormal chains are built into helices and damage many molecules (dominant negative effect).
questions.why: Type I collagen has two pro-alpha1 chains (COL1A1) and one pro-alpha2 chain (COL1A2). Glycine must occupy every third position because only this smallest amino acid fits in the center of the triple helix. A glycine substitution produces a chain that still joins helices but kinks them, and because each molecule contains two alpha1 chains, about three quarters of the molecules are abnormal. This dominant negative effect causes the severe forms. A null allele removed by nonsense-mediated decay leaves only normal chains in half the amount, which gives the milder type I form.
whyNot: This is the dominant negative mechanism of glycine substitutions, which cause the more severe forms. Her mutant mRNA is destroyed, so no mutant chains are made.
The remaining normal allele does not fully make up the loss. If it did, she would have no fractures.
Type I collagen made by fibroblasts and odontoblasts is also affected, which explains her blue sclerae, lax joints, and abnormal teeth.
Correct.

questions.stem: Which of the following deficits should be looked for most carefully in her injured right limb?
options: Inability to extend the wrist and fingers
Inability to abduct the arm at the shoulder
Inability to flex the elbow with the forearm supinated
Inability to spread the fingers apart
approach: Locate the fracture: the middle third of the humeral shaft.
Recall that the radial nerve runs in the radial groove on the back of the humeral shaft at this level.
Predict radial nerve injury: weak wrist and finger extension (wrist drop).
questions.why: The radial nerve winds around the back of the middle of the humerus in the radial groove, with the deep brachial artery. A midshaft fracture can stretch or trap it, causing wrist drop and loss of finger extension at the metacarpophalangeal joints, with sensory loss over the back of the hand. Other classic pairings: surgical neck fracture with the axillary nerve, supracondylar fracture with the median nerve and brachial artery, and medial epicondyle fracture with the ulnar nerve.
whyNot: Correct.
Loss of shoulder abduction suggests axillary nerve injury, which goes with fractures of the surgical neck of the humerus or shoulder dislocation.
Weak elbow flexion with the forearm supinated suggests musculocutaneous nerve injury, which is rare with humeral shaft fractures.
Inability to spread the fingers reflects weak interossei from ulnar nerve injury, as with medial epicondyle fractures.

topics: Nerves at risk with humeral fractures

dx: Classic Ehlers-Danlos syndrome with recurrent shoulder dislocation
case: A 22-year-old woman comes to the emergency department 1 hour after her left shoulder dislocated while she reached overhead to place a box on a shelf. This is her fourth shoulder dislocation since the age of 16 years. She bruises easily, and her mother has similar skin and joint problems. Neither has had arterial or bowel rupture. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows a squared-off left shoulder with the humeral head palpable anteriorly. Her skin is soft and stretches easily, and there are wide, thin, shiny scars over both knees and the forehead. She can place her palms flat on the floor with her knees straight. Diagnosis: classic Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains her skin and joint findings?
options: Glycine substitutions in the type I collagen triple helix
Mutant type III collagen weakening arteries and bowel wall
Mutant type V collagen disrupting type I fibril assembly
Mutant type IV collagen weakening basement membranes
approach: Identify the classic type of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome: stretchy skin, wide atrophic scars, lax joints, and no arterial or bowel rupture.
Recall that classic Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is most often caused by mutations in type V collagen (COL5A1 or COL5A2).
Type V collagen helps control the size of type I fibrils, so its loss makes dermal and ligament fibrils irregular and weak.
questions.why: Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is a group of disorders of collagen structure or processing. In the classic type, mutant type V collagen fails to regulate the assembly of type I collagen fibrils, so dermis and ligaments contain irregular, weak fibrils. The result is soft, stretchy skin that splits easily and heals with wide, thin scars, joint hypermobility with dislocations, and easy bruising from fragile small vessels. The vascular type, caused by type III collagen mutations, carries the risk of arterial, bowel, and uterine rupture.
whyNot: Glycine substitutions in type I collagen cause the severe forms of osteogenesis imperfecta, with fractures and blue sclerae.
Type III collagen mutations cause vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, with thin, translucent skin and rupture of arteries, bowel, or uterus. Her family has none of these.
Correct.
Type IV collagen mutations cause Alport syndrome, with kidney disease, hearing loss, and eye findings.

questions.stem: Because of her easy bruising, a nutritional cause of weak collagen is considered before genetic testing. In vitamin C deficiency, which of the following steps of collagen synthesis is impaired?
options: Cross-linking of collagen fibrils by lysyl oxidase
Glycosylation of hydroxylysine residues in the rough ER
Cleavage of propeptides from procollagen outside the cell
Hydroxylation of proline and lysine in the rough ER
approach: Recall the order of collagen synthesis: chain synthesis, hydroxylation, glycosylation, triple helix formation, secretion, propeptide cleavage, then cross-linking.
Identify the step that needs ascorbate: prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases.
Predict the result: unstable helices and fragile vessels, causing bleeding gums, perifollicular hemorrhage, and easy bruising.
questions.why: Collagen chains are made in the rough endoplasmic reticulum as repeats of Gly-X-Y. Prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases then add hydroxyl groups, and they need vitamin C (and iron) as cofactors. Hydroxyproline stabilizes the triple helix, and hydroxylysine is needed for glycosylation and later cross-linking. In scurvy, underhydroxylated collagen forms unstable helices, so vessel walls are fragile and wounds heal poorly. Other steps fail in other diseases: propeptide cleavage in some Ehlers-Danlos types and cross-linking in Menkes disease.
whyNot: Lysyl oxidase needs copper. Its failure in Menkes disease, a disorder of copper transport, weakens collagen and elastin.
Glycosylation of hydroxylysine follows hydroxylation and does not itself require vitamin C.
Procollagen peptidases cleave the propeptides outside the cell. Defects in this step cause rare types of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
Correct.

questions.stem: After reduction of her shoulder, which of the following findings would most likely indicate a nerve injury caused by the dislocation?
options: Scapular winging when pushing against a wall
Lateral shoulder numbness and weak arm abduction
Weak wrist extension and numbness of the dorsal hand
Weak elbow flexion and lateral forearm numbness
approach: In an anterior dislocation, the humeral head moves forward and down, below the coracoid process.
The axillary nerve wraps around the surgical neck of the humerus just below the joint capsule and is stretched.
Predict axillary nerve signs: weak deltoid abduction and numbness over the lateral shoulder.
questions.why: The glenohumeral joint trades stability for range of motion. The glenoid fossa is shallow, so the joint depends on the rotator cuff muscles and the capsule and ligaments to hold the humeral head in place. With lax capsular collagen in Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, the head dislocates easily, most often anteriorly. The axillary nerve passes through the quadrangular space and around the surgical neck, so anterior dislocation can stretch it. Injury weakens the deltoid and teres minor and numbs the skin over the lower deltoid.
whyNot: Scapular winging comes from long thoracic nerve injury, which affects the serratus anterior. This nerve runs on the chest wall and is not stretched by anterior dislocation.
Correct.
Weak wrist extension with dorsal hand numbness points to radial nerve injury, usually from a fracture of the humeral shaft.
Musculocutaneous nerve injury can occur with dislocation, but it is much less common than axillary nerve injury.

questions.stem: Six weeks later, she inverts her right ankle while stepping off a curb. There is swelling and tenderness just anterior and inferior to the lateral malleolus, with no tenderness over the bones. The anterior drawer test shows increased forward movement of the foot. Radiographs show no fracture. Which of the following best describes this injury?
options: Sprain of the anterior talofibular ligament
Strain of the fibularis brevis musculotendinous unit
Contusion of the soft tissue over the lateral malleolus
Dislocation of the talocrural joint
approach: Locate the tenderness: anterior and inferior to the lateral malleolus, the site of the anterior talofibular ligament.
A positive anterior drawer test means this ligament is torn or stretched.
An injury to a ligament is a sprain, while a strain affects muscle or tendon.
questions.why: A sprain is a stretch or tear of a ligament. A strain is an injury to a muscle or tendon. A contusion is bleeding into soft tissue from a direct blow, and a dislocation is complete loss of contact between joint surfaces. Inversion with the foot pointed down most often injures the anterior talofibular ligament, and the anterior drawer test checks it. Ligaments heal slowly because they are dense collagen with few fibroblasts and limited blood supply, and the repair scar is weaker than the original ligament. In Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, the lax collagen raises the risk of sprains.
whyNot: Correct.

A fibularis brevis strain would cause pain along the tendon behind the malleolus or at its insertion on the fifth metatarsal, with pain on resisted eversion. A positive anterior drawer test points to a ligament.
A contusion follows a direct blow and causes bruising without joint instability. Her anterior drawer test is abnormal.
A talocrural dislocation would cause obvious deformity and usually a fracture. Her joint surfaces remain in contact.

case: A 10-month-old boy is brought to the physician for a well-child examination. He was born at term to a 27-year-old mother and a 45-year-old father, both of average height, and there is no family history of short stature. His length is below the 1st percentile, and his head circumference is above the 97th percentile. Physical examination shows short arms and legs with redundant skin folds, a trunk of normal length, a prominent forehead, a flat nasal bridge, and short fingers with a gap between the middle and ring fingers. Radiographs show short tubular bones. Diagnosis: achondroplasia.

questions.stem: Which of the following patterns of limb shortening is most characteristic of his disorder?
options: Upper arms and thighs shortened most
Forearms and lower legs shortened most
Hands and feet shortened most
Trunk shortened more than the limbs
approach: Recall that achondroplasia impairs endochondral bone growth at the growth plates.
The proximal long bones (humerus and femur) normally grow the most in length, so they lose the most.
Name the pattern: rhizomelic shortening, with a trunk of near-normal length.
questions.why: Achondroplasia is the most common skeletal dysplasia. All long bones are short, but the proximal segments, the humerus and femur, are shortened most (rhizomelia). The trunk is close to normal length, the head is large with frontal bossing and a flat nasal bridge, and the hands are short with a trident shape. Intelligence is normal. Motor milestones can be delayed in infancy because of low muscle tone and the large head, which is different from cognitive delay.
whyNot: Correct.
Shortening that is worst in the forearms and lower legs is mesomelic. It is seen in other skeletal dysplasias.
The hands are short in achondroplasia, but the most marked shortening is in the proximal segments.
A trunk shorter than the limbs points to a spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia, which affects the spine. In achondroplasia the trunk is close to normal.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains how this child acquired his disorder?
options: Both parents carry one copy of a recessive mutant allele
A new FGFR3 gain-of-function mutation in a sperm cell
An FGFR3 loss-of-function allele inherited with low penetrance
Maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 4
approach: Achondroplasia is autosomal dominant with essentially full penetrance, so an affected parent would show it.
Both parents are of average height, so the mutation is new.
Most new achondroplasia mutations arise in the father's germ cells and become more frequent with advanced paternal age.
questions.why: Achondroplasia is caused by gain-of-function mutations in FGFR3, most often the same glycine-to-arginine change at position 380. FGFR3 normally slows chondrocyte proliferation in the growth plate, and the overactive receptor slows it too much. About 80% of cases are new mutations, and these arise almost always on the paternal chromosome, with risk rising with paternal age. Recurrence risk for these parents is low, but each child of an affected person has a 50% chance of inheriting it.
whyNot: Achondroplasia is autosomal dominant, so carrier parents of average height do not explain it. Two affected parents can have a child with the severe homozygous form.
Correct.
The FGFR3 change in achondroplasia increases receptor activity, and penetrance is essentially complete, so a parent carrying it would be affected.
Uniparental disomy causes disease mainly through imprinting or by unmasking a recessive allele. It is not how achondroplasia arises.

topics: Advanced paternal age and new mutations

questions.stem: If a biopsy of his proximal tibial growth plate were examined, which of the following would most likely be seen?
options: Early closure of the plate with bony bridging across it
Widened hypertrophic zone with unmineralized cartilage
Retained calcified cartilage cores within dense trabeculae
Short, disorganized columns in the proliferative zone
approach: List the growth plate zones from the epiphysis: reserve, proliferative, hypertrophic, calcification, and ossification.
Overactive FGFR3 inhibits chondrocyte proliferation.
Predict a short, poorly organized proliferative zone, so less cartilage is made for bone to replace.
questions.why: Long bones grow in length when chondrocytes in the proliferative zone divide and stack into columns, then enlarge in the hypertrophic zone before the matrix calcifies and is replaced by bone. In achondroplasia, overactive FGFR3 slows proliferation and hypertrophy, so the columns are short and disorganized and bone length suffers. Intramembranous bone formation is spared, so the skull vault and the width of the long bones develop normally, which helps explain the large head. In rickets, the problem is mineralization, so the hypertrophic zone widens with uncalcified cartilage.
whyNot: Early fusion of the growth plate follows trauma, infection, or excess sex steroids. It does not explain disproportionate shortening from birth.
A widened hypertrophic zone with unmineralized cartilage is the growth plate picture of rickets from vitamin D deficiency.
Retained calcified cartilage within dense bone is seen in osteopetrosis, where osteoclasts fail to remove it.
Correct.

questions.stem: His parents ask whether his limbs formed abnormally early in pregnancy. His limbs have every normal segment and differ only in length. In the embryo, loss of which of the following signals during limb bud outgrowth would produce limbs that end abruptly, with proximal segments present and distal segments missing?
options: Sonic hedgehog from the zone of polarizing activity
WNT7a from the dorsal ectoderm
FGF from the apical ectodermal ridge
HOX transcription factors in limb mesenchyme
approach: Link each signal center to its axis: the apical ectodermal ridge for proximal to distal, the zone of polarizing activity for anterior to posterior, and the dorsal ectoderm for dorsal to ventral.
Truncation of the distal limb means proximal to distal outgrowth stopped.
The apical ectodermal ridge drives that outgrowth through FGF signaling.
questions.why: The apical ectodermal ridge is a thickened rim of ectoderm at the tip of the limb bud. It secretes FGFs that keep the underlying mesenchyme dividing, so the limb grows out from proximal to distal. Removing the ridge early truncates the limb near the body, and later removal truncates it more distally. Sonic hedgehog from the zone of polarizing activity sets the anterior to posterior pattern (extra expression causes polydactyly), HOX genes give each segment its identity, and thalidomide disrupts outgrowth to cause phocomelia. His limbs are complete but short because his defect lies in later growth plate function.
whyNot: Sonic hedgehog from the zone of polarizing activity patterns the limb from thumb side to little finger side. Its ectopic expression causes extra digits.
WNT7a from the dorsal ectoderm sets the dorsal to ventral pattern, such as nails on the back of the digits.
Correct.
HOX genes give segments their identity. Their mutations change the shape or number of segments, as in synpolydactyly, instead of stopping outgrowth.

case: A 67-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 3-year history of pain in her right knee. The pain worsens with walking and climbing stairs and eases with rest. She has about 15 minutes of stiffness after waking and after sitting for long periods. She worked as a mail carrier for 30 years. Her body mass index is 34 kg/m2. Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination of the right knee shows bony enlargement, crepitus with movement, medial joint line tenderness, a mild varus deformity, and a small, cool effusion. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate is 12 mm/h (normal 0 to 30). Synovial fluid analysis shows a leukocyte count of 700/mm3 (noninflammatory, below 2,000) and no crystals. Radiographs show medial joint space narrowing, osteophytes, and subchondral sclerosis. Diagnosis: primary osteoarthritis of the right knee.

questions.stem: Three years later, she undergoes total knee arthroplasty. The medial femoral condyle has a smooth, polished, ivory-like surface. Which of the following best explains this appearance?
options: Calcium pyrophosphate crystals deposited within cartilage
Inflamed synovial pannus spreading across the cartilage
Chalky urate deposits coating the articular cartilage
Exposed subchondral bone polished by friction
approach: Trace the sequence of osteoarthritis: proteoglycan loss, fibrillation and cracking of cartilage, then full-thickness cartilage loss.
Once cartilage is gone, bone rubs on bone.
The rubbing polishes and thickens the subchondral bone, called eburnation.
questions.why: Osteoarthritis starts with chondrocyte injury from age, load, and obesity. Chondrocytes release enzymes that break down proteoglycan and type II collagen, the cartilage softens, splits along its surface (fibrillation), and wears away. When subchondral bone is exposed, friction polishes it into a smooth, ivory-like surface (eburnation), and the bone beneath thickens (sclerosis) and may form cysts. Osteophytes grow at the joint margins. Her medial compartment carries the most load, especially with a varus knee, so it wears first.
whyNot: Calcium pyrophosphate deposition (chondrocalcinosis) occurs in pseudogout. It does not produce a polished bone surface.
Pannus is inflamed, proliferating synovium that erodes cartilage in rheumatoid arthritis. Her synovial fluid is noninflammatory.
Chalky white urate deposits on joint surfaces are seen in chronic gout. Her synovial fluid contained no crystals.
Correct.

questions.stem: Examination of her hands is most likely to show which of the following?
options: Hard bony enlargement of the distal interphalangeal joints
Ulnar deviation and swelling of the metacarpophalangeal joints
Sausage-shaped swelling of an entire digit with nail pitting
Soft, warm, symmetric swelling of both wrists
approach: Osteoarthritis in older women often involves the hands as well as weight-bearing joints.
Bony osteophytes at the distal interphalangeal joints are Heberden nodes, and at the proximal interphalangeal joints Bouchard nodes.
Separate these hard, cool swellings from the soft, warm synovitis of inflammatory arthritis.
questions.why: Osteoarthritis causes pain that worsens with use, morning stiffness under 30 minutes, and asymmetric involvement of weight-bearing joints such as the knee and hip. In the hands it targets the distal and proximal interphalangeal joints and the base of the thumb, producing hard bony swellings: Heberden nodes at the distal joints and Bouchard nodes at the proximal joints. The metacarpophalangeal joints and wrists are usually spared. Radiographs show joint space narrowing, osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis, and cysts.
whyNot: Correct.
Ulnar deviation with metacarpophalangeal swelling is typical of rheumatoid arthritis, which also causes prolonged morning stiffness.
A sausage digit with nail pitting points to psoriatic arthritis.
Soft, warm, symmetric wrist swelling indicates synovitis from an inflammatory arthritis such as rheumatoid arthritis.

questions.stem: Loss of proteoglycan is one of the earliest changes in her articular cartilage. Which of the following components of normal articular cartilage is mainly responsible for resisting compressive loads?
options: A dense capillary network supplying the chondrocytes
Type I collagen fibers aligned parallel to the surface
Water bound by the sulfated chains of aggrecan
Elastic fibers that recoil after the load is removed
approach: Recall the structure of aggrecan: a core protein with many chondroitin sulfate and keratan sulfate chains, attached in large numbers to hyaluronan.
The negatively charged sulfate groups attract cations and water, which swell the matrix.
Bound water resists compression like a cushion, and losing proteoglycan lets cartilage deform and wear.
questions.why: Articular cartilage is hyaline cartilage made of type II collagen and proteoglycan, mainly aggrecan. Each aggrecan molecule carries many chondroitin sulfate and keratan sulfate chains and attaches to hyaluronan to form huge aggregates. Their dense negative charge draws in water, which resists compression and is pushed out and drawn back with each load. Cartilage has no blood vessels, so chondrocytes rely on diffusion from synovial fluid, which helps explain why damaged cartilage repairs so poorly.
whyNot: Articular cartilage is avascular. Chondrocytes receive nutrients by diffusion from synovial fluid.
Articular cartilage collagen is type II, and collagen fibrils mainly resist tension. Type I collagen is found in bone, tendon, and fibrocartilage.
Correct.
Elastic fibers are found in elastic cartilage of the ear and epiglottis. Hyaline articular cartilage relies on bound water to resist compression.

questions.stem: To reduce her knee pain, she begins a 12-week program of progressive resistance exercise for the quadriceps. Which of the following changes in the trained muscle is most likely?
options: Higher mitochondrial density, mainly in type I fibers
Enlargement of existing fibers, mainly type II
Formation of many new fibers by fiber splitting
Conversion of most type II fibers to type I fibers
approach: Separate the two training types: endurance training improves oxidative capacity, and resistance training builds strength.
Strength gains come mostly from adding myofibrils to existing fibers.
Type II fibers show the most hypertrophy with resistance training.
questions.why: Type I fibers are slow, oxidative, red, and rich in mitochondria and myoglobin, and they resist fatigue. Type II fibers are fast and glycolytic, generate high force, and fatigue quickly. Heavy resistance training enlarges existing fibers by adding actin and myosin filaments, with the largest gains in type II fibers, so strength increases. Endurance training instead increases mitochondria, capillaries, and oxidative enzymes, mainly in type I fibers. Early strength gains in the first weeks also come from better neural recruitment.
whyNot: More mitochondria in type I fibers is an adaptation to endurance training, such as long-distance running or cycling.
Correct.
In adult humans, strength training enlarges existing fibers. New fiber formation contributes little or nothing.
Training changes fiber subtypes only slightly, mostly within type II fibers. It does not convert most fast fibers into slow fibers.

dx: Postmenopausal osteoporosis with vertebral compression fracture
case: A 71-year-old woman comes to the physician because of sudden midback pain that began 5 days ago when she lifted a bag of groceries. She has lost 4 cm of height over 10 years. Menopause occurred at the age of 47 years, and she has never taken hormone therapy. She has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 40 years. Her body mass index is 19 kg/m2. Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows thoracic kyphosis and point tenderness over the T12 spinous process. Serum studies: calcium 9.4 mg/dL (normal 8.5 to 10.5), phosphorus 3.6 mg/dL (normal 2.5 to 4.5), alkaline phosphatase 82 U/L (normal 40 to 120), and PTH 38 pg/mL (normal 10 to 65). A radiograph shows anterior wedging of the T12 vertebral body. Diagnosis: postmenopausal osteoporosis with a vertebral compression fracture.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the accelerated bone loss that began after her menopause?
options: Lower PTH secretion, which slows osteoblast-driven bone formation
More RANKL and less osteoprotegerin, increasing osteoclast formation
Defective mineralization of osteoid from vitamin D deficiency
Less calcitonin secretion, which releases osteoclasts from inhibition
approach: Identify the hormonal change: loss of estrogen at menopause.
Recall that estrogen restrains bone resorption by lowering RANKL and raising osteoprotegerin.
Without estrogen, more osteoclasts form and live longer, so resorption outpaces formation.
questions.why: Osteoblasts and stromal cells express RANKL, which binds RANK on osteoclast precursors and drives their formation and activity. Osteoprotegerin is a decoy receptor that blocks RANKL. Estrogen lowers RANKL, raises osteoprotegerin, reduces bone-resorbing cytokines such as IL-1, IL-6, and TNF, and shortens osteoclast life span. After menopause these brakes are lost, and trabecular bone, as in the vertebrae, thins fastest. Her early menopause, smoking, and low body weight add to the risk, as do low peak bone mass and aging.
whyNot: Low PTH would reduce bone resorption and would not explain bone loss. Her PTH is normal.
Correct.
Defective mineralization is osteomalacia. In osteoporosis the bone that remains is normally mineralized, and her calcium, phosphorus, and alkaline phosphatase are normal.
Calcitonin plays only a small role in adult bone. People who lose it after thyroidectomy do not develop osteoporosis from that loss.

questions.stem: Dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry shows a lumbar spine T-score of minus 3.1. Which of the following best describes the meaning of this value?
options: 3.1 standard deviations below the mean for women of her age
31 percent below the mean bone mass for women her age
31 percent below the young adult female mean bone mass
3.1 standard deviations below the young adult female mean
approach: A T-score compares bone density with the peak value of healthy young adults of the same sex.
It is expressed in standard deviations.
A Z-score is the measure that compares with people of the same age.
questions.why: The T-score is the number of standard deviations a patient's bone density lies above or below the mean for healthy young adults of the same sex. A T-score of minus 1 or higher is normal, between minus 1 and minus 2.5 is osteopenia, and minus 2.5 or lower is osteoporosis. A fragility fracture of the spine or hip establishes osteoporosis on its own, whatever the T-score. Typical findings are vertebral compression, hip, and distal radius fractures, height loss, and kyphosis, with normal serum calcium, phosphate, and alkaline phosphatase.
whyNot: Comparison with people of the same age and sex is the Z-score, which is used for premenopausal women, men under 50, and children.
This mixes two errors: the comparison group of the Z-score and a percentage instead of standard deviations.
T-scores are expressed in standard deviations. A percentage loss cannot be read directly from the score.
Correct.

questions.stem: Which of the following sets of serum findings would have pointed to osteomalacia from vitamin D deficiency instead of osteoporosis?
options: Low calcium, low phosphate, high alkaline phosphatase, high PTH
Normal calcium, normal phosphate, high alkaline phosphatase, normal PTH
High calcium, low phosphate, high alkaline phosphatase, high PTH
Low calcium, high phosphate, high alkaline phosphatase, high PTH
approach: Vitamin D deficiency lowers intestinal absorption of calcium and phosphate.
Low calcium triggers secondary hyperparathyroidism, and PTH makes the kidney waste phosphate.
Poorly mineralized osteoid stimulates osteoblasts, which raises alkaline phosphatase.
questions.why: In osteoporosis, bone mass is low but its mineral is normal, so calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, and PTH are all normal, as in this patient. In vitamin D deficiency osteomalacia, calcium is low or low-normal, phosphate is low, PTH is high, and alkaline phosphatase is high. Primary hyperparathyroidism raises calcium and lowers phosphate. Renal osteodystrophy lowers calcium and raises phosphate because the failing kidney cannot excrete phosphate or make calcitriol. Paget disease raises alkaline phosphatase alone.
whyNot: Correct.
An isolated high alkaline phosphatase with normal minerals and PTH is the pattern of Paget disease of bone.
High calcium with low phosphate and high PTH is primary hyperparathyroidism, usually from a parathyroid adenoma.
Low calcium with high phosphate and high PTH is renal osteodystrophy from chronic kidney disease.

topics: Lab patterns in metabolic bone disease

questions.stem: She has taken warfarin for 6 years for atrial fibrillation. Which of the following modifications of a bone matrix protein is most likely reduced by this drug?
options: Lysyl oxidase cross-linking of type I collagen fibrils
Hydroxylation of proline residues in type I collagen
Gamma-carboxylation of glutamate in osteocalcin
Phosphorylation of serine residues in osteopontin
approach: Recall that warfarin blocks vitamin K epoxide reductase, so active vitamin K is depleted.
Vitamin K is the cofactor for gamma-carboxylation of glutamate residues.
Apply this beyond clotting factors: osteoblasts make osteocalcin, a vitamin K dependent protein.
questions.why: Vitamin K is needed by gamma-glutamyl carboxylase, which adds a carboxyl group to specific glutamate residues. This creates gamma-carboxyglutamate (Gla), which binds calcium. Clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X depend on it, and so does osteocalcin, a bone matrix protein made by osteoblasts that binds hydroxyapatite. Warfarin and vitamin K deficiency leave osteocalcin undercarboxylated. Other cofactors matter for bone and muscle too: copper for lysyl oxidase, vitamin C for collagen hydroxylation, and magnesium for PTH secretion.
whyNot: Lysyl oxidase needs copper and is impaired in Menkes disease and copper deficiency.
Proline hydroxylation needs vitamin C and fails in scurvy. Warfarin does not affect it.
Correct.
Osteopontin phosphorylation is done by kinases and does not depend on vitamin K.
